about: Where agenttrace/messages.py (A) and agenttrace/refcount.py (B) differ, with a judgement of each group. The judgement was written for the v2.2.0 rule on 2026-11-16 and is kept below as written. The rule changed in v2.3.0: the block 'v2_3_0' (2026-11-22) gives the current crosscheck numbers (release 11 and 11) and marks what has not been judged again. Judged by reading samples of each group; not every row was read. The judgement of the v2.1.0 run (which had 173 of B's extras unread) is replaced by this file.

v2_3_0.read_this_first: The rule changed after the judgement below was written (R13a: a record cut inside a verb is joined with the record that completes it; R2: the answer kinds of a tool server are not actions; R18a: a tool call that names its place operates on it; R38b: the reader's later output). The crosscheck was run again on 22 November 2026 and this block records what that run shows and what was NOT judged again. Everything outside this block is the v2.2.0 judgement, kept as written; where the two differ, this block is the current one.

written_content_test.note: R38a and R38b: neither implementation passes any of the 11 deliveries.

deliveries_added_since_v2_2_0.judged: NOT JUDGED. Found by both implementations after R13a joined R0022674 with R0022675 (a POST to .../commit/main cut inside 'POS). The audit label is still 'unclear': it was given on 2026-11-16 when the call could not be read, and nobody has read the joined text as a labeller. Both implementations were given R13a by the same team from the same statement, so their agreement on these two is not a second opinion.

NOT JUDGED. Found by both implementations after R13a joined R0022674 with R0022675 (a POST to .../commit/main cut inside 'POS). The audit label is still 'unclear': it was given on 2026-11-16 when the call could not be read, and nobody has read the joined text as a labeller. Both implementations were given R13a by the same team from the same statement, so their agreement on these two is not a second opinion.

operations.judged: NOT JUDGED AGAIN. The six groups come out with the same sizes as on 2026-11-16, and all 24 of the 24 rows read then still differ in the same way (same reading on each side). The list of operations of the 2026-11-16 run was not kept (crosscheck.json is not tracked), so it cannot be shown that the two sets of 262 are the same operations; the rows were not read again. The judgements under swarm_traces_release.operations.groups are therefore carried over from the v2.2.0 rule, not repeated for the v2.3.0 rule.

v2_3_0.other_datasets_note: Deliveries agree on every dataset. Counts that differ from the v2.2.0 block: {"sample langfuse_observations.json": {"v2_2_0": 8, "v2_3_0": 9}, "sample mcp_toolcalls.jsonl": {"v2_2_0": 17, "v2_3_0": 3}, "sample otel_genai_spans.json": {"v2_2_0": 6, "v2_3_0": 8}}. They changed with the v2.3.0 rule. R2 and R18a concern tool-call logs (the server is no longer a party; a call that names its place operates on it) and are the likely cause, but the cause was not traced and the rows were not read.

written_content_test_where_the_verdicts_.judged: PARTLY. docs/counting-rule.md gives the cause as read from the code: the main implementation's R38a passes a delivery on the host name left over when the place's pattern is cut out of its URL (demo swarm) or on the page's own name (wiki logs), which is part of the place's address and not content; the second implementation leaves both out. That is a fault of the main implementation's R38a, unchanged in v2.3.0 and not fixed. The rows (listed in crosscheck.json, content_test.verdict_differs) were not read one by one.
written_content_test_where_the_verdicts_.R38b: On the wiki logs B passes 262 deliveries by R38b and A 258; A passes the other 4 by R38a already, so the verdicts agree there.

v2_3_0.mutation_testing: Run again on 2026-11-22 on messages.py with R13a and R38b (reports/integrity/mutation.json: 1,570 of 1,656 mutants killed; 78 of the 86 survivors judged equivalent by one reader, 8 not). That run is of the main implementation only and says nothing about the differences listed here.

read_this_first.deliveries: On every dataset the two implementations now find the same deliveries (Swarm Traces release 9 and 9, collusion.wiki logs 9,867 and 9,867, demo swarm 164, benign swarm 1, and the 8 format samples).
read_this_first.not_independent: That agreement was reached by changing B while reading where it differed from A on the release. Before the change B found 191 deliveries against A's 9 (7 in both; disagreement 96.4%, threshold 10%). Every change to B is one of the faults below, judged against the written rule (docs/counting-rule.md) and not by copying messages.py, but the release disagreements were read, B was changed more than a dozen times against them, and the release was run after each change. So agreement on the release is no longer an independent check of messages.py there; it shows that two tokenisations of the same rule can be brought to agree, and that B's first result (191) was B's own fault. The independent evidence is the earlier agreement of the two on the wiki logs, the demo swarm and the samples (unchanged by this work, still exact) and the 262 operation-level differences listed below, which were not removed.
read_this_first.what_it_does_not_show: Both implementations were written by the same team from the same document. They agree on what the rule says; neither shows the rule is the right one. B was also tuned on the very records the audit labelled, so its agreement with the audit labels (5 of the 9 true, 4 unclear) is not a second opinion either.

before_this_work.rule: v2.2.0 rule in messages.py, refcount.py as it stood (it implemented R1 to R34 only)
before_this_work.cause: Redaction removes quote marks, so the tokenizer in B paired quotes wrongly and lost the call that held the place. Of the 184 extras, in 127 the reader's operation was a POST (a commit) that B took for a read (2 more where messages.py had no operation at all there); in 44 the writer's operation was a place that is only read (a name used again as an object key `u:`, a call stretched through a redaction into the next request, a body that names the place) that B took for a write; 10 were the LFS upload probe (R6b was not in B); 1 was the reader holding the writer's token (R23a). I read samples of each group (2 to 6 rows each) in both records. None of the 40 extras the earlier reviewer read was a message; that reading (0% to 8.8%) agrees with this.

changes_to_refcount: R6a (a mention followed by /paths-info is a read), R6b (an LFS upload batch is a write only if no earlier download batch named its object and a later record sends it as an lfsFile or with a PUT; no visible object id: not counted), R13 inside the verb (record ends in `method:'POS`), R23a (a read record that holds the writer's own token as a whole word, for a write whose actor is a token), R38 (the written-content test; output has deliveries_write_then_read, deliveries_reader_uses_content, uses_content and shared_terms), R39 (carried by the pack's full-path board pattern).

A request call is judged from the raw text when the tokens cannot be trusted: the call that starts before the mention with no `;` or line break between (R8), ending at its parenthesis, the next request call or 600 characters (R16); a call that has been closed before the mention is not the call that holds it.

The tokens are only used when the quote before the mention opens its string in the token list; otherwise the code is tokenised again from the name being assigned, or from the request call that starts before the mention.
A name's later uses skip object keys with the same spelling (`u:` in `{s:r.status,u:r.url}`) and, when the tokens show nothing, are followed on the raw text (R9).
A `;` ends the arguments of a call (a `body=` assignment after a cut call was read as its verb).
R14: with no call, the nearest verb counts only within the same statement; a place in the body or data argument of a call is data (read by default).
R12: a request written as data is read although its `{` starts a line.
R15: the second argument that is a bare name is looked up as an object literal, or as a parameter of the wrapper function whose callers (500 characters after) carry the verb.

written_content_test.note: neither implementation finds a delivery whose reader quotes a term of the writer's record that is found in at most 5 records.

operations.note: 262 single operations out of about 16,300 still differ. None changes a delivery. They are listed by group with a judgement; groups are by what each side says about the same (place, record).

groups.judgement: B's rule, by design: a request call left open at the end of a record with no verb is not counted (R13), however far the end is; messages.py reads it as a request without a method (R8, a read by default). Neither is shown wrong: the verb may or may not have been cut. No delivery depends on it.

B is nearer the written rule. Most are a name held in a shell variable or in code with escaped quotes (U='...'; curl "$U"), or a name formatted into a call (urlopen(Request(b%i))): R9 says a name passed to a call is a read, and counting-rule.md already lists these shapes as ones messages.py does not recognise. No delivery depends on them: each is a read with no earlier write by another actor, or the write is also not a delivery.

Mixed, and each side is wrong in some. B is right where a helper takes the address and a body (p('...place...', '{"key":...}') posts: counting-rule.md lists this as messages.py reading it as a read by default). B is wrong where the method is a ternary on a variable that is null (method:D?'POST':'GET' with D=null is a GET); it sees a verb and a body. No delivery depends on them.

B is right in the ones read: the place is named in a pasted dataset card line (path: reference://...::https://huggingface.co/datasets/X) or in a string that is printed (t+='[WEBHOOK HOST 10]'), and the POST that messages.py takes as its verb belongs to another statement (R14 nearest verb within 160 characters). B stops the window at a `;` or a line break. Not every row was read.

Rule difference in R6b. All are the same object (one oid) in LFS upload batches with x_hf copy-source in the body. messages.py counts the batch as an upload that goes up because it accepts upload_file or uploadId as the later sending; the spec text names only an lfsFile in a commit and a PUT, which B follows. Whether the other signals show the object going up is the open question; no delivery depends on it (neither side links these writes to a reader).

One record cut at 96 characters: `('POST','https://[SERVICE HOST 9]/https://huggingface.co/api/datasets/[HF REPO 21]`. B takes the POST as the verb of the call; messages.py does not count a mention at the end of a record (R13). Not decided.

known_differences_still_in_the_code: Listed at the head of agenttrace/refcount.py. They do not change a delivery on any dataset here; they would on traces shaped differently.
